Lesson Overview: Academic and Craft Vocabulary

Lesson Focus

Lesson 3: Academic and Craft Vocabulary

Primary Standard: MLA.CW.WR.05 — Academic and Craft Vocabulary.

Supporting Standards: MLA.CW.COM.03 — Voice and Tone; MLA.CW.WR.07 — Connotation, Denotation, and Style.

What You Will Learn

  • Use accurate craft terms to explain evidence, not simply label devices.
  • Distinguish denotation from connotation and justify meaning through context.
  • Explain how two writing choices work together to create a reader effect.
  • Revise a passage deliberately and defend the revision with precise terminology.

Why This Matters

Creative writing helps you communicate ideas, experiences, and perspectives with purpose. Each lesson strengthens your ability to read like a writer, make deliberate craft choices, revise thoughtfully, and explain how those choices affect a reader. These skills build creative confidence, clear communication, and responsible participation in a writing community.

What You Will Do

  • Learn and apply the lesson vocabulary.
  • Follow step-by-step instruction and study worked examples.
  • Practice through interactive checks and guided application.
  • Complete Independent Work to apply the lesson skills.
  • Complete a separate Checkpoint to demonstrate your understanding.

Lesson Workflow

  1. Complete Pages 1–4 in order.
  2. Complete Page 5 and submit it with your Page 2 vocabulary in Notebook Evidence Submission.
  3. Complete Page 6 and submit it separately in Checkpoint Submission.
  4. Review TOR feedback, correct errors, and resubmit any work scoring below 80%.
  5. Complete the assessment listed after the lesson. A score of at least 80% is required.

page.title: Vocabulary and Definitions
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 1 | Lesson 3 | Page 2 of 6

Vocabulary and Definitions

Notebook Task

Record every core term and its complete meaning in your notebook. Submit these vocabulary notes with your Independent Work as Notebook Evidence. Use the examples to see how each term works in context. Reference glossary terms do not need to be copied.

TermMeaningExample
dictionDeliberate word choice, including precision, formality, sound, and association.The writer replaces “walked” with “crept” to create tension.
denotationA word’s literal dictionary meaning.The denotation of “storm” is severe weather.
connotationEmotional, cultural, or personal associations carried beyond literal meaning.“Home” can suggest comfort beyond its literal meaning.
imageryLanguage that creates sensory experience through sight, sound, touch, taste, smell, or movement.Cold rain tapped the window and soaked her sleeves.
syntaxThe arrangement and rhythm of words, phrases, clauses, and sentences.One knock. Silence. The short syntax slows the moment.
figurative languageNonliteral language—such as metaphor, simile, or personification—used to create comparison, emphasis, or layered meaning.The floorboards groaned beneath his steps.
detailA selected fact, action, object, or observation that develops character, setting, tone, conflict, or meaning.A cracked photograph hints at the family’s history.
structureThe organization and sequence of parts in a sentence, passage, scene, poem, or complete work.The letter’s contents are withheld until the final paragraph.
styleA recognizable pattern formed by recurring choices in diction, syntax, imagery, detail, voice, and structure.Brief sentences and precise images create a spare style.
reader effectThe thought, feeling, inference, expectation, or interpretation produced by a craft choice or pattern.The delayed answer makes readers anticipate what comes next.

Drag and Drop — Craft Vocabulary in Action

Apply the ten terms to writing situations. Drag a word into a box, or click a word and then its destination. Select Check, read the feedback, and use Retry when needed. This practice is optional and ungraded; it does not block progress or need to be submitted.

Keep the Levels Separate

FocusTermExample
Chosen wordDictionReplacing “walked” with “crept.”
Literal meaning / associationDenotation / connotation“Thrifty” and “stingy” both concern spending little, but suggest different judgments.
Sentence arrangementSyntax“One knock. Silence.” isolates moments.
Information orderStructureA letter’s contents are withheld until the final paragraph.
Recurring pattern / responseStyle / reader effectRepeated brief statements form a spare style; delayed information may create anticipation.

Pause and Try

Can “The floorboards groaned” demonstrate both diction and figurative language? Explain before opening the feedback.

Check your thinking

Yes. “Groaned” is a chosen word, and it gives floorboards a human-like vocal action: personification, a form of figurative language. Choose the term most useful to your explanation, then show its effect in context. You do not need to list every possible label.

Reference Glossary — Understand, Do Not Copy

TermMeaning here
simile / metaphor / personificationA simile compares using like or as; a metaphor presents one thing as another; personification gives a nonhuman thing a human quality or action.
fragment / clauseA fragment is an incomplete sentence used deliberately in some creative writing. A clause contains a subject and verb.
pacing / inferencePacing is how quickly or slowly events seem to unfold. An inference is a reasonable conclusion from evidence, not a confirmed fact.
tone / purposeTone is the attitude communicated by language. Purpose is what the writer intends readers to understand, feel, question, or do.
sill / cumulative / spareA sill is a window ledge. Cumulative means building by adding parts. A spare style uses relatively few, carefully chosen words.

Creative Writing | Unit 1 | Lesson 3 | Page 3 of 6

Lesson: From Evidence to a Useful Craft Explanation

Start with What the Words Do

Imagine a classmate says, “Your paragraph has imagery.” That may be accurate, but it does not tell you what to preserve or improve. Today we will turn a label into useful reasoning. Read a short passage first for its situation. Only then choose the terms that help explain how it works.

Our goal is not to find a device in every sentence. It is to make a claim a reader can test against the text. We will move from evidence → accurate term → specific effect → purpose, then use that explanation to revise.

Step 1 — Separate What Happens from What You Infer

Read: “The dog crept toward the porch, stopping whenever the screen door sighed.” What happens? A dog approaches and repeatedly stops when the door makes a sound. What might we infer? The dog seems cautious. We do not know that someone has hurt it or that the house is dangerous. Keep that limit in mind: a convincing explanation does not need an invented backstory.

Step 2 — Quote Small; Name Precisely

EvidenceAccurate termWhy it fits
“crept”DictionThe writer selected a verb for slow or careful movement.
“crept” suggests caution hereConnotationThe association is supported by repeated stopping.
“the screen door sighed”Personification; figurative languageA nonhuman object is described with a human-like action.
The dog stops repeatedlySelected detailThis action supports our interpretation of caution.

Notice that one phrase can support more than one term. “Sighed” is diction and personification. Use the label that makes your reasoning clearer; do not stack labels to sound academic. Personification does not mean the door is literally alive.

Pause and Try

Would “The dog crept toward the porch, trying not to wake the baby” support exactly the same inference as the original?

Pause: say or jot your answer before opening the explanation. This is optional, ungraded practice, not a submission.

Check your thinking

No. “Crept” still denotes careful movement, but the added context supports consideration for the sleeping baby rather than fear of the door. Connotation depends on the surrounding evidence; a word is not a fixed code for one emotion.

Step 3 — Explain the Connection with Because

Now move past “This is personification.” Try: The door’s “sigh” makes the setting seem almost responsive to the dog. Because the dog stops at that sound, the description makes an ordinary approach feel uncertain. The second sentence connects two choices. It does not merely repeat the definition of personification.

Ask yourself: What specifically does the reader notice, question, anticipate, or infer? “It makes readers interested” is too general. “It makes readers anticipate what is behind the door” identifies an expectation the text supports. Say “may,” “suggests,” or “invites” when describing interpretations—not every reader reacts identically.

Pause and Choose: Evidence, Term, and Effect

Text: “The clock swallowed the last minute. I kept my hand on the unopened envelope.”

Which explanation would help a writer understand what to preserve? Read both complete responses, choose A or B, and then open your choice.

A. This is imagery, diction, syntax, and detail, so the writing is very powerful.
Not the best explanation. This answer stacks labels without showing where each one appears or what it does. “Powerful” is too vague to guide revision. A useful analysis selects relevant evidence, names the choice accurately, and explains a specific effect.
B. “Swallowed” treats time as something consuming the moment; the unopened envelope keeps information withheld, creating pressure.
✓ Correct—stronger explanation. This response quotes exact evidence, identifies figurative language and a selected detail, and explains how they work together. It stays within the evidence: pressure is supported, but the envelope’s contents remain unknown.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

Reasoning chain: evidence → accurate term → specific effect → careful limit.

Step 4 — Distinguish Syntax from Structure

Syntax concerns how words and sentences are arranged. Structure concerns how parts of a passage are organized. They can overlap, but they are not interchangeable.

VersionWhat I noticeEffect I can justify
“I lifted the lid. Slowly.”The fragment isolates one adverb.The pause draws attention to hesitation; the short unit can slow this moment.
“I lifted the lid and saw the letter and reached for it before anyone could stop me.”Linked clauses accumulate in one sentence.The continuous chain can quicken this action rather than relax it.
A passage reveals the letter’s contents only in its final paragraph.Information is withheld until the end.The structure sustains a question across the passage.

A paragraph break is not automatically a sentence fragment. Before naming a fragment, check whether the sentence lacks a complete grammatical structure. Before saying “fast” or “slow,” explain what the arrangement makes you experience.

Pause and Choose: Syntax or Structure?

Observation: A story withholds the letter’s contents until its final paragraph.

Which explanation uses the most precise craft term and reasoning?

A. The syntax creates suspense because the letter comes at the end.
Not the best explanation. Syntax concerns the arrangement of words and sentences. This observation concerns where information appears across the whole passage, so the answer uses the wrong level of analysis.
B. The structure sustains suspense by delaying essential information until the final paragraph.
✓ Correct—precise reasoning. This answer identifies the passage-level organization as structure and explains how withholding information maintains a question for the reader.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

Step 5 — Use Your Analysis to Revise

Start with “The corridor was quiet.” Suppose we want a welcoming rather than threatening atmosphere. First choose a target. Then coordinate two choices: “Warm light rested along the corridor, and someone had left a chair beside the open door.”

“Warm” and “rested” suggest comfort; the available chair and open door imply welcome. These choices reinforce each other. Changing only “quiet” to “nice” would name an attitude without giving the reader a concrete experience. Keep the central situation—a quiet corridor—while changing how it is presented.

Model rationale: I replaced the general adjective with visual imagery of warm light and selected the detail of an open door. Together they invite a reassuring interpretation because the space seems prepared for a visitor rather than closed against one.

Pause and Try

Change “The corridor was quiet” to suggest unease. Add one sensory detail and one action or object. Keep the corridor quiet.

Pause: say or jot your answer before opening the explanation. This is optional, ungraded practice, not a submission.

Check your thinking

One possibility: “Cold light trembled along the corridor; every door had been fastened from the outside.” The visual detail and unusual fastening may create unease without adding a loud event. “Trembled” personifies the light. Other versions can work: explain the effect your own evidence supports, and avoid claiming this is the only correct answer.

Step 6 — Test Your Terminology and Your Claim

  1. Point to it: Can I quote the exact evidence?
  2. Check the label: Does this term describe the choice, or am I guessing?
  3. Explain the relationship: How do my two choices reinforce or complicate each other?
  4. Respect the limit: Have I invented a fact the text does not establish?
  5. Read the revision: Does it create the intended effect through language, not just announce an emotion?

Common Mistakes — Repair the Explanation

Weak moveUseful repair
“It has lots of devices.”Choose two relevant choices, quote them, and explain their relationship.
“A long sentence always slows the pace.”Inspect this sentence’s clauses, punctuation, and action before naming an effect.
“The word means danger in every passage.”Use denotation to check meaning and context to justify an association.
“The author wants every reader to feel scared.”Describe a likely purpose with evidence and allow for different responses.
“I corrected spelling, so I changed the style.”Editing fixes mechanics; revision changes meaning or effect. Explain an actual craft change.

page.title: Worked Example
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 1 | Lesson 3 | Page 4 of 6

Worked Example: Notice, Explain, Revise

Watch the Teacher’s Decisions

We will use three short models, not three unrelated lists of devices. In each, I will establish the task, choose evidence, explain how two choices work together, and test a revision. Read the model answer only after following the reasoning that produces it.

Example 1 — Diction and Character

Text: “The dog crept toward the porch, stopping whenever the screen door sighed.”

1. Set the task. Explain how the description makes the approach uncertain. Then make it welcoming while keeping a dog approaching a porch and hearing a door.

2. Select evidence. I choose “crept” and “stopping whenever.” Both describe movement. I also notice “sighed,” but I will not claim that this alone proves danger.

3. Think through the connection. “Crept” suggests care or caution in this context. Repeated stopping reinforces hesitation. The door’s human-like “sigh” makes the ordinary sound seem significant to the dog.

4. Complete model analysis. The cautious connotation of “crept” is reinforced by the selected detail of repeated stopping. Personifying the door as something that “sighed” makes the setting seem responsive, so the approach feels uncertain. The sentence suggests hesitation without establishing its cause.

5. Write and defend the revision. “The dog trotted toward the porch and lifted its nose as the screen door whispered open.” “Trotted” gives the movement more ease, and lifting the nose suggests curiosity instead of stopping. “Whispered” keeps a soft sound. Together the diction and action invite a gentler reading, although context could still change that interpretation.

Pause and Choose: A or B

Why is “The dog is definitely frightened because it was abandoned” not a strong explanation of Example 1?

Pause: say or jot your answer before opening the explanation. This is optional, ungraded practice, not a submission.

Pause and Choose: A or B

Which response gives the stronger evidence-to-reasoning explanation? Choose before opening either response.

A. This response is stronger because it sounds more creative and includes more detail.
Weaker response. This claim is vague. It does not identify exact evidence, explain a reader effect, or connect the choice to the writer’s purpose.
B. The sentence suggests caution, but it gives no history of abandonment. An interpretation should explain the actual language and respect what remains unknown. The stronger response connects “crept” and repeated stopping without inventing a cause.
Stronger response. This answer uses specific evidence, explains the reasoning, and connects the choice to the purpose of the model.

Retry: Close your first choice and open the other. Compare both explanations before continuing.

Example 2 — Imagery, Detail, and Information Order

Text: “Orange dust clung to the sill, and every footprint ended before the locked room.” A sill is the ledge at the bottom of a window.

1. Set the task. Explain how two setting details create a question. Do not solve the mystery.

2. Select evidence. I mark “orange dust” and the footprints ending before the locked room. The color creates visual imagery. The footprints are a selected trace of someone’s movement.

3. Test my first claim. I might write “The house has been empty for years.” But dust alone cannot prove how long it has been there, and footprints complicate a simple claim of emptiness. I will qualify the interpretation.

4. Complete model analysis. The visual imagery of “orange dust” suggests neglect, while the footprints indicate that someone has moved through the space at some point. Placing the “locked room” at the end directs attention to a boundary. These details invite a question about access rather than establish who was there or when.

5. Revise for reassurance. “Orange dust clung to the sill, but fresh footprints led to an open room where two cups steamed.” The contrasting conjunction “but,” the open room, and the warm sensory detail counter the initial neglect. This changes the setting details deliberately; it is not merely a synonym swap.

Pause and Choose: A or B

In Example 2, why is “visual imagery” a more precise label for “orange dust” than “syntax”?

Pause: say or jot your answer before opening the explanation. This is optional, ungraded practice, not a submission.

Pause and Choose: A or B

Which response gives the stronger evidence-to-reasoning explanation? Choose before opening either response.

A. The phrase appeals to sight through color and a visible substance. Syntax could describe how the whole sentence is arranged, but it does not identify the sensory work of those two words. Choose the label that explains the evidence you are actually discussing.
Stronger response. This answer uses specific evidence, explains the reasoning, and connects the choice to the purpose of the model.
B. This response is stronger because it sounds more creative and includes more detail.
Weaker response. This claim is vague. It does not identify exact evidence, explain a reader effect, or connect the choice to the writer’s purpose.

Retry: Close your first choice and open the other. Compare both explanations before continuing.

Example 3 — Syntax and the Timing of Discovery

Text: “One step. Then another. Then the door. Behind it, the radio continued playing to an empty room.”

1. Set the task. Explain how the sentence pattern controls the approach and discovery. Then create a more continuous movement without changing the empty room or playing radio.

2. Name the actual pattern. The first three units are fragments: incomplete sentences. “Then” repeats. The final sentence gives more information and includes a subject and verb.

3. Explain the effect. Each stop isolates a stage of the approach. The longer final sentence releases the discovery, but the radio playing without a visible listener leaves a question. An empty room is not proof of danger; the arrangement invites uncertainty.

4. Complete model analysis. The repeated fragments make readers attend to each step separately, slowing the approach in this passage. The structural decision to reveal the empty room last postpones the discovery. The radio’s continuing sound then makes that absence noticeable, sustaining uncertainty instead of fully resolving it.

5. Revise and compare. “I crossed to the door and opened it on a radio still playing in an empty room.” Linked actions replace the isolated stages, so the movement feels more continuous. The important facts stay, but the syntax reduces the stop-and-start approach. This revision changes pacing; it does not guarantee that the room now feels safe.

A Visual Comparison

ModelTwo choices working togetherWhat the explanation avoids
DogCautious verb + repeated stoppingInventing a past event to explain hesitation.
Dust and footprintsSensory imagery + a contrasting trace of movementClaiming a date or identity that is not given.
Steps and radioRepeated fragments + delayed discoveryTreating short sentences as automatically fast.

Pause and Try

Write one sentence explaining a change you could make to the radio model. Name the choice and its likely effect.

Pause: say or jot your answer before opening the explanation. This is optional, ungraded practice, not a submission.

Check your thinking

For example: “I would place ‘an empty room’ first, changing the structure so readers know the discovery before the approach; this reduces uncertainty about what is behind the door.” A different revision is acceptable when the term fits the change and the claimed effect follows from it.

page.title: Independent Work
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 1 | Lesson 3 | Page 5 of 6

Independent Work: Use Craft Language Precisely

Purpose and Directions

Apply academic and craft vocabulary to analyze a complete passage, make one focused writing choice, and explain it precisely. Complete every numbered task and submit this work with your vocabulary notes in Notebook Evidence Submission. Quality matters more than length.

Draft for Workshop: “The Hallway”

The final bell released the building all at once. Lockers snapped shut, shoes squeaked across the tile, and voices rushed toward the exits. Mara moved against the current with an unopened envelope pressed beneath her notebook. At Room 214, she stopped. The hallway emptied. The envelope seemed heavier when no one was watching.

1. Notice and Name

Complete three rows. Use a precise lesson term only when it accurately describes the evidence.

Exact languagePrecise craft termEffect on meaning or tone
Record your three evidence-based notes in your submission.

2. Choose the Stronger Analysis

Record A or B, then explain in two or three sentences why your choice uses terminology and reasoning more accurately. The answer is not revealed on this page.

A. The passage has imagery, syntax, diction, and suspense because it uses many writing techniques.

B. The crowded sound details contrast with the short sentence “The hallway emptied,” shifting the pace and isolating Mara so the unopened envelope gains importance.

3. Apply the Craft in Your Writing

Write a six-to-eight-sentence micro-scene in which a character carries or hides an important object. Before drafting, name your intended reader effect. Use three lesson terms to plan three purposeful choices, but do not force techniques that do not serve the scene.

4. Revise and Explain

Replace one vague or unnecessary sentence with a more purposeful version. Show the original and revision, then explain in two or three sentences which craft term accurately names the change and how it strengthens the intended effect.

Before You Submit

  • I completed every numbered task.
  • My terms accurately describe the quoted evidence.
  • My A/B explanation connects evidence, craft, and effect.
  • My original scene uses purposeful choices, and I revised one sentence.

page.title: Checkpoint
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 1 | Lesson 3 | Page 6 of 6

Checkpoint: Academic and Craft Vocabulary

Your Purpose

Independently analyze a new source and apply academic and craft vocabulary in organized original writing.

Complete all four parts. A score of at least 80% is required.

New Source: “Under the Awning”

The awning clicked in the wind. Imani watched the empty intersection, rehearsing the apology without speaking it. When the signal changed, she stayed on the curb. The red hand vanished; the white figure appeared; still, her shoes held their place.

Term support: An awning is a covering that extends above a doorway or window. Subtext is meaning suggested beneath spoken words or visible actions.

1. Analyze the Source

  1. Identify one example of imagery and one example of subtext. Quote the exact evidence and explain how each functions.
  2. Explain how the repeated traffic signal affects pacing and meaning. Use the terms evidence, craft choice, and reader effect accurately.

2. Choose and Defend

Record A or B, then defend your choice in 3–4 sentences using source evidence and a lesson concept. Explain why the other response is weaker.

A. The symbolism proves Imani committed a serious crime and is afraid of punishment.
B. The repeated signal may symbolize opportunities to act, but the passage does not establish why Imani is apologizing.

No answer is revealed before submission. Your choice and reasoning are graded.

3. Create and Organize

Task: Write a 275–375 word scene in which a character hesitates at a familiar boundary. Correctly apply at least four lesson terms through the writing and analysis.

Required organization:

  1. Opening—begin with a concrete image that establishes the boundary and situation.
  2. Development—use imagery and one additional craft technique to build subtext.
  3. Turning point—change the pacing when something forces the character to respond.
  4. Closing—end with a symbolic action or object whose meaning is supported by the scene.

4. Revise and Explain

Annotate four craft terms beside exact passages in your scene. Revise one passage where the named term is inaccurate or ineffective, then explain the correction.

Before You Submit

  • Both analysis questions use exact source evidence.
  • Your A/B defense applies the lesson concept and addresses both choices.
  • Your original writing follows the required organization and demonstrates the lesson skill.
  • Your revision is meaningful and your explanation identifies its effect.
  • Your work is original, complete, and carefully proofread.

80% Mastery Requirement

If your score is below 80%, review the identified weakness and follow your TOR’s directions for correction and resubmission.

TOR Help
Contact your Teacher of Record if you need clarification, feedback, or support before submitting your work.
